assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's 2001-2003 proposal of the magic wavelength, which removes the optical-lattice light shift, together with Ye's realization of clocks with extraordinary stability and accuracy, is a clear and original invention. It improved the best clock performance by orders of magnitude, enables relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants, and strongly supports redefinition of the second. It is exactly measurement physics whose reach is set by what can be measured and how accurately.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the decisive conceptual invention and first demonstration in strontium. Ye led the implementation that pushed stability and systematic uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and the quantum many-body clock work. The two-name configuration is clean; other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley) contributed demonstrations but not the founding idea. Pairing is fair.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced in Sr, Yb and other species at many national laboratories and compared across continents; the interpretation is stable and the technology is mature. Timely, with no sign of premature recognition.
uncertainties: I note Ye trained in John Hall's laboratory, where I also spent a research period; this is a disclosed professional connection, not a stake in the outcome.
The relative weight of Ye versus Katori, and of contributions from other groups to the accuracy milestones, may be debated; I rely on my recollection of the history, which I have not verified here.
Whether the Academy prefers a clock prize that also includes frequency-comb or ion-clock lineage is open (Hall and Hänsch were recognized in 2005, Wineland in 2012).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turns matter-wave coherence into an inertial and constant-measurement tool: gravimeters, gyroscopes, gravity-gradiometers, and determinations of the fine-structure constant and G. It is a conceptually clear, widely adopted precision-measurement platform with direct links to tests of the equivalence principle and gravitational-wave proposals.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group demonstrated early atom interferometers with material gratings and Bordé proposed the light-pulse Ramsey-Bordé geometry; Kasevich and Chu demonstrated light-pulse interferometers with sensitivity to gravity. Chu already shared the 1997 prize for cooling and trapping, which complicates adding him but leaves a three-person set among the listed names. Other names such as Mlynek, Keith, Chu and Rasel are not in the credited set; the allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Strong replication and commercial and field use; however the most compelling fundamental-physics payoffs (equivalence-principle tests at high precision, space missions) are still maturing, so the recognition is solid but slightly less decisive than for clocks.
uncertainties: Credit division between the Pritchard, Bordé and Kasevich lineages is historically contested and I have not verified details.
Overlap with the 1997 cooling prize and with the 2001 condensate prize could be raised in committee.
Fundamental-physics reach beyond metrology is not yet delivered.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion quantum gate proposal and the subsequent neutral-atom, Rydberg and optical-lattice proposals created the conceptual blueprint for quantum computing and simulation with controlled atoms. The importance and originality are very high, and experiments in many laboratories have implemented the ideas.
assessment.attribution: Two names with a close and long-running collaboration and a shared decisive contribution; the configuration is clean. Experimentalists such as Wineland (already honoured in 2012) and Blatt demonstrated gates but are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally validated for twenty-five years and now central to commercial and academic programmes. Recognition is timely, though some may argue that the 2012 and 2022 prizes already covered part of the territory.
uncertainties: The scope of the prize (theory only, versus including experiments) could be debated.
Overlap with B010 and B023 involving the same laureates means a choice of how to frame the citation.
The tension with the 2025 circuit prize and with earlier quantum-information recognition is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realization of the Mott-insulator transition, Fermi-Hubbard physics and quantum-gas microscopes turned ultracold atoms in optical lattices into programmable analog simulators of strongly correlated matter. The result is a major experimental platform that has changed how many-body physics is studied, with clear and lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Bloch and Greiner built on the Greiner et al. Mott-insulator experiment and the later quantum-gas microscope; Esslinger contributed fermionic lattice experiments and the Fermi-Hubbard realization. Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard scheme with Jaksch; if he is excluded here, the proposal credit is unresolved and a combined prize with B014 might be more natural. I choose the three experimentalists but this allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Widely confirmed across many groups; interpretation is stable and the platform is mature. Recognition is timely, but the 2001 condensate prize and Hänsch-style frequency control are context rather than overlap.
uncertainties: The decisive credit for the first Mott-insulator observation versus later developments (microscopy, fermions) is not obvious.
Whether the Academy regards simulation results as discovery or technique is unresolved.
Missing Zoller and Jaksch in this proposed set could be criticised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state quantum sensor with nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and biological applications. It is a tangible example of using single quantum systems to measure fields and forces with high sensitivity, and the impact on sensing and quantum-network nodes is broad.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group reported optically detected magnetic resonance on single NV centres in 1997; Jelezko extended this to coherent control and spin-photon interfaces; Lukin developed nanoscale magnetometry and quantum-register ideas. Others (Hanson, Awschalom, Yacoby, Budker) are not in the credited names, so the three-name set omits notable contributors.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed and increasingly applied; however, the applications are still evolving and the choice between sensing, quantum registers and networks as the prize theme is not settled.
uncertainties: The leading claim for the first single-spin detection versus subsequent coherent control may require careful allocation.
The breadth of applications makes the prize citation harder to bound.
The credited set excludes strong NV contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Radiation-pressure coupling of light and mechanical motion led to sideband cooling to the quantum ground state, optomechanically induced transparency, squeezed mechanical states and entanglement. It underlies ultrasensitive force and displacement detection and is conceptually clear, linking quantum optics and precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Vahala, Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer made central early contributions in microresonator optomechanics and quantum-regime demonstrations; other contributors such as Harris, Painter, Lehnert, Teufel and Schwab, and Braginsky as a conceptual forerunner, are not in the credited names. The three-person selection is plausible but leaves clear gaps.
assessment.maturity: Quantum-ground-state demonstrations were reproduced in several platforms, though practical sensing impact beyond gravitational-wave detectors is still emerging. The field may be slightly early for a prize.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit across platforms (microwave, nano-mechanical, microtoroid) makes a three-person prize uncertain.
Whether the discovery is a unified phenomenon or a collection of techniques is not settled.
Overlap with the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum phenomena in circuits may be raised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Electromagnetically induced transparency and slow and stopped light show quantum-coherence control of absorption and dispersion, with consequences for nonlinear optics, quantum memories and light-matter interfaces. The concept is elegant and lasting, and the experiments are striking.
assessment.attribution: Harris developed and demonstrated EIT; Hau demonstrated ultraslow light and stopped light in a condensate; Imamoglu contributed early theoretical proposals and nonlinear optics at low light levels. Other contributors (Fleischhauer, Lukin, Arimondo, Alzetta, Phillips) are not in the credited names. Because my own research lies in slow light and coherent storage in crystals, I regard my judgement here as potentially biased and weigh it modestly.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely used, but the field is mature enough that interest is dispersed in later applications; the timing is reasonable but the case is less compelling than metrology-oriented candidates.
uncertainties: I disclose a research-area overlap with slow light and quantum memories; I have not independently verified any priority claims.
The best credited triplet is arguable given Fleischhauer, Lukin and Imamoglu contributions.
The Academy may view EIT as an enabling technique rather than a stand-alone discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed vacuum injection reduces quantum noise in interferometers, and Caves's 1981 proposal for quantum-limited interferometry is directly realized in gravitational-wave detectors. The idea is simple and important, with demonstrated sensitivity gains, and it is a clear case of quantum resources improving measurement.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the key theoretical proposal for squeezed-light interferometry; Kimble and colleagues produced the first experimental squeezed states (the 1985 four-wave-mixing result was by Slusher et al., not in the credited set); Schnabel advanced the practical implementation in GEO600 and LIGO. The credited set omits Slusher, Walls, Wu and others, so the allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in operating detectors since 2011 and routinely used; however the discovery chain is spread over several decades and the scientific significance is strongly tied to the already-honoured gravitational-wave detection.
uncertainties: Whether squeezing is an independent prize-worthy invention or an enhancement of the 2017 detection is debatable.
Credit history is diffuse and I have not verified the details.
Several important experimentalists are not among the credited names.
